messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a 42-year-old farmer of Vietnamese descent, married for eighteen years to Liên, with two children. Three years ago, their youngest son, then aged five, developed bacterial meningitis. The illness struck fast. Minh remembers the night they rushed him to the emergency room—the bright lights, the smell of antiseptic, the way his son’s small arm looked with the IV line taped down, the skin around the insertion point slightly swollen and pale. That image—the thin limb, the tape, the needle—lodged itself into him like a splinter. Now, whenever Minh catches a glimpse of a child’s bare arm, or a medical bracelet, or even the curve of a wrist in a certain light, his chest tightens and his mouth goes dry. His mind yanks him back to that hospital bed as if no time has passed.

The worst hours came after midnight. The doctors had told them to wait, that the next few hours would decide everything. Minh sat in a dark corner of the room, the only light coming from the monitors. His son lay motionless, the IV dripping, the machine beeping at steady intervals. That darkness—the quiet, the lying still, the helpless waiting—has become something Minh cannot face. When evening comes and Liên turns off the lights, he feels a crawling dread. He has come to believe that if he lies down in the dark, he will be pulled back into that moment, forced to live it all over again. So he stays up. He watches television until the channels sign off, or he sits on the porch staring at the empty yard, waiting until sheer exhaustion drags him into a shallow, restless sleep around three in the morning. Liên has asked him why he will not come to bed, but he cannot explain it. He only knows that the dark feels unsafe.

Certain songs can undo him as well. During those hospital nights, a volunteer played a soft lullaby over the intercom at eight o’clock, meant to soothe the children. Now, if Minh hears that melody—or any song that resembles it—his throat closes up. Last month at the feed store, a radio played a ballad with a similar tune, and Minh had to leave mid-transaction, leaving his supplies on the counter. Since then, he avoids the feed store altogether, sending Liên instead.

The memories themselves arrive without warning: a fragment of his son’s hand gripping the bedrail, the sound of a beeping monitor, the smell of hand sanitizer. They flash into his mind and vanish, but while they last, they feel utterly real. Minh is certain that the event is not over—it is still happening, just beneath the surface of his everyday life. He finds himself checking his son’s breathing at night, studying his arms for any sign of illness, scanning the faces of other children at the market. This hypervigilance drains him.

He has stopped visiting his neighbors. He used to enjoy sitting at the coffee shop after the morning chores, but now he avoids people entirely. He worries that someone might ask how his son is doing, or that he will see a child who reminds him of those weeks. His farming work has suffered: he refuses to go to the fields after dusk, even during harvest season when the light fades early. Liên has had to take over the evening watering and the late checks on the livestock, which has created a quiet strain between them.

What finally brought Minh to therapy was an incident last week. He fell asleep on the couch in the late afternoon from sheer exhaustion, and when he woke, the room was dim. He saw his own hand resting on his chest—the veins visible, the fingers curled—and for a terrible moment he was certain it was his son’s arm with the IV, and he screamed. Liên ran in and found him trembling. She insisted he see someone. Now, sitting in a clinician’s office, Minh is terrified that he will never feel normal again, but somewhere underneath that fear is a thin thread of hope—that maybe he can learn to let the night fall without being dragged back into the worst hours of his life.
